Table 1. Back labial: velarized and without rounding, more accurately [pˠ] as in Hughes (2020); ʷ follows the Oceanist convention (p. 654). The voiceless labials are relatively uncommon (p. 676). Word-finally the front/back contrast of labials is neutralized; the final labial matches a preceding labial, else it is front after e, i, ɨ and back elsewhere (pp. 655-656). Voiceless stops are phonetically long and voiced stops short, but this length is not phonological (p. 656). Stop voicing is neutralized word-finally and is unstable word-initially in fast speech (p. 656).

Table 1. Front labial, palatalized (p. 654). Not frequent; word-final [p] only in epep, gabõp and in loans such as dorop 'rope', dowip 'whip' (p. 655 and fn. 4). Word-finally the front/back contrast of labials is neutralized; the final labial matches a preceding labial, else it is front after e, i, ɨ and back elsewhere (pp. 655-656). Voiceless stops are phonetically long and voiced stops short, but this length is not phonological (p. 656). Stop voicing is neutralized word-finally and is unstable word-initially in fast speech (p. 656).

Table 1. Coronal (p. 654). Affricate allophone before /i/, ranging from lightly affricated [tˢ] to [tʃ], heavier in younger speakers; also before [i] from /ɨ/ fronted between front consonants (pp. 654, 671). Hughes (2020) treats the affricates as separate phonemes (p. 673). Voiceless stops are phonetically long and voiced stops short, but this length is not phonological (p. 656). Stop voicing is neutralized word-finally and is unstable word-initially in fast speech (p. 656). Initial t (ts) can be pronounced voiced (p. 656).

Table 1. Unrounded counterpart of kʷ; the contrast is kept word-finally (p. 655). Voiceless stops are phonetically long and voiced stops short, but this length is not phonological (p. 656). Stop voicing is neutralized word-finally and is unstable word-initially in fast speech (p. 656).

Table 1. Rounded velar: unlike the back labials, the secondary articulation is rounding; ɡ and ŋ have no rounded counterpart, and the contrast with k is kept word-finally (pp. 654-655). Infrequent; written q (p. 676).

Table 1. Glide, called the palatal glide; realized with significant frication, commonly from [j] to [ʝ] to [z], heavier in younger speakers (p. 654). Contrasts with the semivowel i̯ (ei̯u 'seven' : eju 'three', p. 661); no gemination, but phonetically long compared with the semivowel (p. 657). A predictable epenthetic i̯ stands before it (p. 662). A front consonant for vowel allophony (p. 670). Hughes (2020) treats j, w as fricatives and the semivowels as the glides (p. 654 fn. 2).

Surface semivowel, the non-syllabic counterpart of the vowel i: stress placement suggests that vowels and semivowels are complementary (p. 661), and the diachronic paper says the semivowels are in complementary distribution with the corresponding vowels i, u (2022b: 684). It stands next to a vowel: after one (é.i̯u 'seven'), also as the offglide of the diphthongs ei̯, æi̯, oi̯, ɑi̯ (ŋei̯n 'child'), and before one (i̯ǽ.i̯o 'native banyan'); contrast syllabic i in i.bí.a 'lump'. Its non-syllabic status is clear only where it would be stressed if syllabic (p. 661). A predictable epenthetic i̯ stands before the glide j (p. 662). It contrasts with the glide j (ei̯u 'seven' : eju 'three') and with u̯ (p. 661); j is fricated and phonetically longer (pp. 654, 657). Hughes (2020) calls i̯, u̯ glides and treats j, w as fricatives (p. 654 fn. 2).
